title: Industrial-scale production and loading of rocket propellant off Earth

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an integrated plant that turns resources available beyond Earth into rocket propellant, prepares and stores that propellant to a vehicle’s requirements, transfers it into a flight tank, and supplies a load that the vehicle actually uses. The target is sustained operation over months and production measured in tons. Demonstrating the chemistry alone would establish only one part of this capability. The MOXIE report grounds a Mars oxygen pathway and describes a future system intended to fill a human-mission propellant tank.

Scope synthesis: production of oxygen alone counts because oxygen serves as rocket oxidizer, although the vehicle would still need fuel from another source. Depending on the vehicle, preparing the product could require purification, compression, liquefaction, and temperature-controlled storage before loading. Lunar or asteroid plants fit the same concept in principle, but their resource extraction and processing pathways are not demonstrated by the supplied Mars evidence. The defining advance is the complete resource-to-flight supply chain.

Milestone synthesis: a first substantial flight load, a second independently completed production-and-departure campaign, and eventual production of hundreds of tons per year represent successive levels of the same capability. They do not require separate concept entries. The historical annual-output target is retained as a possible later scale, without treating it as an achieved result or an established minimum for completion.

significance.text: Locally produced propellant could reduce the mass that missions must transport from Earth. The MOXIE report connects resource use on Mars to substantial mission-mass reductions and proposes oxygen production for a future human return mission. The benefit depends on the mission architecture, the locally supplied share of the propellant, and the mass and power infrastructure required to produce it; the supplied evidence does not establish a universal mass fraction for crewed Mars missions.

Impact synthesis: local refueling changes where propellant enters a mission and how much mass must pass through earlier burns. The rocket equation remains unchanged. An oxygen-producing plant could remove the need to deliver some oxidizer from Earth while leaving fuel delivery and other logistics in place. A successful integrated campaign would establish one locally supplied flight. Repeated campaigns could establish a dependable departure service, provided the plant, vehicles, and supporting infrastructure remain available.

Conditional downstream possibilities include repeated surface-to-orbit transport and propellant depots supporting interplanetary travel. These require additional storage, delivery, transfer, and vehicle infrastructure; they do not follow automatically from a single plant demonstration. Self-sustaining settlements, large metal structures, and a broader space economy would also need capabilities beyond propellant production, including other forms of mining, manufacturing, and maintenance.

Interpretive analogy: a network of off-Earth propellant suppliers could change transport logistics in a way comparable to historical coaling networks, by allowing vehicles to replenish consumables along their routes. The analogy describes a potential transport system, not an outcome demonstrated by MOXIE. Its usefulness is limited by the demanding resource, power, thermal, storage, and transfer conditions of space operations.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is sustained integration at flight-relevant scale: producing tons of usable propellant, conditioning and retaining it, loading a vehicle, and completing a flight that consumes it. MOXIE demonstrated oxygen production on Mars, while its report presents the tank-filling successor as future work. Scaling production must address power supply, atmospheric compression, filtration, thermal management, and operational control together.

Dust and thermal cycling need careful treatment rather than being described simply as unsolved failures. The MOXIE report identifies robustness against both as a lesson from the experiment. That experience supports the Mars oxygen pathway, but it does not establish the lifetime, maintenance needs, or reliability of a much larger plant operating for months. Component robustness and sustained system availability are different engineering questions.

Engineering synthesis: the complete system must match production rate to available power, manage heat and pressure, meet engine-compatible product specifications, and prevent unacceptable losses during storage and transfer. For a vehicle requiring liquid oxygen, oxygen generation must be coupled to liquefaction and cryogenic handling. Autonomous operation must detect faults, recover where possible, and preserve the accumulated inventory. These are integrated engineering barriers; the supplied evidence does not identify a need for a new chemical principle.

Resource-pathway synthesis: a plant using lunar ice or asteroid material would additionally need to locate accessible feedstock, extract it, and process material of variable composition before producing flight propellant. The supplied MOXIE evidence addresses atmospheric carbon dioxide processing on Mars. It does not establish the feasibility, performance, or present operational status of those other resource pathways.

current_state.text: In their 2024 Tenth International Conference on Mars abstract, Michael H. Hecht, Jeffrey A. Hoffman, P. Steen, and the MOXIE team report that MOXIE aboard Perseverance completed 16 oxygen-production runs without failures, met its success criteria, and achieved twice its required production rate. This is a demonstrated Mars oxygen-production result. The supplied review does not substantiate a specific grams-per-hour figure, so no absolute production rate is assigned here.

The same report describes an envisioned successor using at least 20 kW, operating for about a year on Mars, and filling a propellant tank with up to 30 tons of oxygen. These numbers describe a proposed human-scale system, not measured output from a completed plant. The report’s demonstrated small-scale performance provides a technical foundation, but does not itself demonstrate ton-scale production, liquefaction, flight-tank loading, or subsequent flight use.

The evidentiary basis is an identified two-page conference abstract whose retained text was complete and untruncated, with no recorded extraction issues. It remains a summary rather than a full technical report. Figure 1 was not visually inspected in the supplied review, and no conclusions here depend on interpreting it. The supported performance statements are reported team results, without an independent replication record supplied.

Evidence boundary as of 2026-11-01: the supplied material does not establish whether the proposed successor has since been built, whether any vehicle has been loaded with propellant manufactured off Earth, or whether lunar ice has been processed into flight propellant. The freshness record contains no evidence resolving those questions. Accordingly, the integrated innovation is not presented as achieved, while worldwide claims that it has never occurred remain unestablished by this record. The absence of such evidence does not invalidate MOXIE’s dated results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed first demonstration: a plant on the Moon or Mars produces at least 10 metric tons of oxygen or fuel from local resources, conditions and stores it to the receiving vehicle’s requirements, transfers it into a flight tank, and supplies the load used for ascent or a documented major maneuver. Ten metric tons is a proposed threshold, not an established standard. Its scale is motivated in part by the MOXIE report’s envisioned tank containing up to 30 tons of oxygen; the report does not prescribe the 10-ton threshold.
completion_criteria.label: At least 10 metric tons of local propellant used in flight

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification: the demonstration should provide a traceable accounting of local feedstock, production, product quality, storage losses, transferred mass, and propellant consumed in flight. Measurements should distinguish locally manufactured inventory from propellant delivered from Earth. Operating records should report duration, power consumption, interruptions, maintenance, and external assistance, so that the demonstrated level of autonomy and practical infrastructure burden can be assessed.
completion_criteria.label: Traceable propellant accounting and operating records document infrastructure burden

completion_criteria.text: Proposed repeatability test: complete a second production-and-departure campaign, documenting replenishment of the consumed inventory and the condition of the plant afterward. This would demonstrate repeatability across two campaigns. Broader industrial reliability would require additional operating evidence across relevant environmental conditions, maintenance cycles, and production demands. Finite demonstrations establish the breadth actually tested; they do not establish universal reliability across sites, resources, or vehicle types.
completion_criteria.label: Second production-and-departure campaign documents inventory replenishment and plant condition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: an oxygen-only demonstration should state the source of the vehicle’s fuel, and a Mars atmospheric-processing demonstration should not be generalized to lunar mining. A later plant sustaining hundreds of tons per year would establish greater throughput within the same concept. Neither the first flight nor that annual production target alone would demonstrate economic competitiveness, a complete depot network, or settlement self-sufficiency.
completion_criteria.label: Propellant demonstrations state fuel sources and limits of applicability

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ROC-01, “Sustained air-breathing combined-cycle flight to orbital speed,” and ROC-02, “Beamed-energy launch of a useful payload into orbit,” pursue different ways of supplying propulsion during launch. ROC-08 instead supplies propellant for a vehicle’s subsequent use. These approaches could coexist in a transport architecture, but successful air-breathing flight or beamed-energy launch would not demonstrate local propellant manufacture and loading.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-03, “A directed-energy lightsail accelerated to a substantial fraction of light speed,” and ROC-06, “A plasma-magnet sail that takes useful delta-v from the solar wind,” obtain momentum through interactions external to a conventional propellant-burning engine. ROC-08 concerns supplying consumable propellant. A broader mission could combine these capabilities, but the sail demonstrations and the resource-to-flight demonstration remain distinct.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-04, “Open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket with high thrust and multi-thousand-second specific impulse,” and ROC-05, “Fission-fragment rocket with direct conversion of fragment momentum into thrust,” concern propulsion mechanisms and engine performance. ROC-08 concerns propellant supply and flight integration. Compatibility would depend on each engine’s required working material and operating conditions; a successful oxygen plant would not establish either nuclear propulsion concept or automatically supply its needs.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-07, “An operational momentum-exchange tether that moves payloads between orbits,” transfers momentum to payloads through a tether system. ROC-08 makes and loads propellant. Both could reduce material that must be delivered from Earth within a suitable architecture, but they require different demonstrations. Cryogenic storage and transfer are enabling capabilities for some ROC-08 implementations; demonstrating either alone would leave local production and flight use unproven.

unresolved_issues: Whether an integrated off-Earth propellant plant or flight-loading demonstration occurred by 2026-11-01 is unresolved by the supplied freshness record.
The supplied evidence does not establish the current status of lunar ice extraction and conversion into flight propellant, or comparable asteroid operations.
MOXIE’s absolute production rate and cumulative oxygen output are not established in the supplied review; twice the required rate does not supply those quantities.
The successor’s continuous operating performance, maintenance needs, liquefaction and storage performance, and flight-transfer integration remain unestablished here.
The proposed 10-metric-ton threshold and two-campaign test would need mission-specific justification before serving as acceptance criteria for a particular program.
The equivalence to a documented historical industrial-production call remains unverified; the hundreds-of-tons annual target is retained only as a proposed later scale.
The supplied record does not establish comparative economics or the infrastructure requirements for a depot-based transport network.

brief.title: Making and loading rocket propellant beyond Earth
possible: A spacecraft could leave the Moon or Mars using rocket propellant made there. A local plant would produce it over months, prepare and store it, then load a vehicle that actually uses it in flight.
Repeated production could support regular departures. Making oxygen locally would count, because rockets use it alongside fuel, even if that fuel still came from Earth.
why: Missions could carry less mass from Earth by making some of their propellant at their destination. That could reduce the cost and complexity of exploration, including the return journey for astronauts on Mars.

sources.cited_for: Small demonstration plants have combined propellant production with automatic operation.
sources.not_established: This does not establish sustained production beyond Earth or use of the product in flight.

sources.cited_for: Large transfers of very cold liquid oxygen have been tested in low gravity.
sources.not_established: The test did not establish a supply chain from local resource extraction to flight use.

demonstrated start-up operation and thermal stability of all components during long-term

sources.cited_for: Key production components have operated under simulated Mars conditions.
sources.not_established: Separate component tests do not establish a complete plant operating on Mars.

shown: The MOXIE team has demonstrated small-scale oxygen production on Mars, completing 16 runs without failures. Its proposed successor would fill a rocket’s oxygen tank, but that larger plant remains future work.

NASA Glenn and SpaceX report a separate advance in moving liquid oxygen between tanks in low gravity. Production and transfer have each progressed, but the complete local-resource-to-flight chain remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A plant must produce tons of usable propellant over months while managing power, heat, faults and maintenance.
The product must meet the vehicle’s requirements and survive storage and loading without unacceptable losses.
A vehicle must consume the locally made load in flight, and the plant must replenish it for another departure.

milestones.label: A flight uses at least 10 metric tons made locally
milestones.explanation: A Moon or Mars plant would have to make, prepare, store and load that amount for ascent or a documented major maneuver. This would demonstrate the complete supply chain at substantial scale.

milestones.label: Measurements account for propellant and operating demands
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to track local inputs, product quality, losses, loading and flight consumption, alongside power, maintenance and outside help. This would reveal the plant’s practical demands and locally supplied contribution.

milestones.label: A second campaign replenishes propellant and supports another departure
milestones.explanation: Another production-and-departure campaign would have to replenish the consumed inventory and document the plant’s condition afterward. This would demonstrate repeatability across the campaigns tested.

milestones.label: Demonstrations identify fuel sources and limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to identify fuel sources and the resources and sites they apply to. Even later output of hundreds of tons annually would establish throughput, without proving competitive costs or settlement self-sufficiency.

uncertain: The amount of propellant and repetition needed for convincing acceptance criteria depend on the mission.
Mars atmospheric processing does not settle whether lunar ice or asteroid material can reliably supply flight propellant.
The costs and infrastructure needed for a wider network of refueling sites remain unresolved.

page.title: In-situ propellant production and refuelling
page.definition: A plant on the Moon or Mars supplies an ascent vehicle at the scale specified in a published human-exploration architecture. It converts local resources into fuel or oxidizer—the substance that reacts with fuel—stores and loads that propellant, and the vehicle consumes it during ascent.

goal.need: ISECG reports that delivering 1 kg to the lunar or Martian surface requires 7.5–13.1 kg of propellant and rocket stages in the architectures it reviewed. NASA’s 2018 Mars ISRU working requirements allocated 22,728 kg of oxygen and 6,976 kg of methane to an ascent vehicle, produced over 434 days. Producing these consumables locally targets that delivery burden; the saving depends on the plant and its supporting infrastructure.

figures.caption: NASA’s 2018 Mars ascent propellant production requirements
figures.note: Working requirements for the Evolvable Mars Campaign: production over 434 days with 24-hour operations. These are design quantities, not demonstrated production.

statements.quote: Produce propellant, consumables, and other usable materials from Martian resources to support human exploration.
demonstrate robotic surface propulsive hopping or ascent with in-situ produced propellants.
statements.context: An example of using products from early lunar resource-utilization demonstrations.

completion.title: An ascent vehicle completes ascent using a mission load of propellant manufactured at its destination.
completion.criterion: An off-Earth plant supplies the complete oxidizer or fuel inventory required by a published human-exploration ascent-vehicle design, meeting that design’s production-duration, purity, phase, storage and transfer requirements. The receiving vehicle completes ascent using that inventory. Oxygen alone can qualify as the locally produced oxidizer; any imported fuel is identified. The test applies separately to the Moon and Mars.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of NASA’s production and refuelling targets, ISECG’s flight-use objective and NASA’s operational-readiness convention.
completion.basis: NASA’s 2019 ISRU vision, 2026 Civil Space Shortfalls, ISECG’s 2021 gap assessment and NASA’s readiness definitions were searched for a single production-to-ascent acceptance test specifying mass, duration and flight use. None was found. This Atlas synthesis combines their mission-scale production, refuelling and operational-use goals without adding a universal tonnage or repetition requirement.

milestones.title: A propellant-production process demonstrates laboratory proof of concept at NASA TRL 3.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the critical production function experimentally, with results supporting analytical predictions, as required at NASA technology readiness level (TRL) 3. Mars: one 1997 plant produced over 125 g of liquid oxygen per six-hour production day and operated autonomously for four diurnal cycles. Moon: experiments used 30 g JSC-2A simulant batches at 950 °C; the 2020 paper reports 96% oxygen removal, with approximately one-third detected in the off-gas and the remainder lost to reactor corrosion.
milestones.set_by: NASA, Technology Readiness Level Definitions, TRL 3; a general hardware criterion rather than a destination-specific production target.
milestones.threshold_quote: Analytical and experimental critical function and/or characteristic proof of concept.

milestones.title: An integrated propellant-production prototype operates in a relevant environment at system TRL 6.
milestones.criterion: Operate an integrated resource-to-propellant prototype in destination-relevant conditions, addressing critical scaling issues and meeting predicted performance at system TRL 6. The 2013 Mars study tested two carbon-dioxide collection/compression systems and one water-electrolysis system separately; it does not demonstrate this integrated result. ISECG’s 2021 lunar assessment records days of hydrogen-reduction and carbothermal tests with simulants in ambient conditions, rather than qualification of the complete plant in lunar conditions.
milestones.set_by: NASA ISRU Project, 2018 overall project goals; NASA’s TRL definitions supply the prototype and scaling conditions.
milestones.threshold_quote: End-to-end ISRU system tests in relevant environment (System TRL 6)

milestones.title: A subscale propellant-production subsystem operates on a lander using local resources.
milestones.criterion: Operate a component or subscale subsystem on a lander using local resources. Mars: one MOXIE instrument completed 16 oxygen-production runs without failures. NASA reported 122 g total, a peak 12 g/h and at least 98% purity, ending on 7 August 2023; these final quantities are from a press release, not peer reviewed. Moon: ESA’s payload target is 50–100 g oxygen, targeting 70% extraction of available sample oxygen within 10 days; no successful lunar-surface production result was located.
milestones.set_by: NASA’s 2019 strategic vision, published NTRS summary; ESA’s 2022 quantitative payload target applies specifically to the Moon.
milestones.threshold_quote: Perform component/subscale subsystem flight demonstrations on small/mid-size landers.

milestones.title: An off-Earth plant produces, stores and loads an ascent vehicle’s mission-scale propellant supply.
milestones.criterion: Produce propellant at human-mission scale, condition and store it, and transfer the required inventory into an ascent vehicle. NASA’s 2019 targets specify 10+ metric tons/year of lunar oxygen and 10–15 metric tons/year of Mars propellant; explicit liquefaction, storage, transfer and refuelling wording is for Mars. A 2025 conference abstract reports multiple metric tons of liquid oxygen transferred between tanks aboard one Starship in low gravity in 2024; it does not demonstrate local propellant production. No integrated destination result was located.
milestones.set_by: NASA’s 2019 strategic vision, published NTRS summary, and 2026 Civil Space Shortfalls, needs 5.08–5.09 and 10.03–10.04; quoted refuelling target is Mars-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: ISRU for propellant production (10-15 MT/yr); Liquefy, store, transfer, and refuel ascent vehicle.

not_found: No single published acceptance test was located that combines human-mission-scale local production, storage, vehicle loading and ascent using the product.
Searches of NASA, ESA and ISECG sources did not locate an integrated lunar or Martian production, loading and ascent demonstration.
No outside requirement for two production-and-departure campaigns was located.
The full 2019 NASA strategic-vision slide deck exceeded the fetch limit; its NASA-published NTRS summary was accessible.

results.finding: MOXIE produced oxygen on Mars over 16 runs without failures.
results.detail: The report describes a small-scale process converting Martian carbon dioxide to oxygen aboard the Perseverance rover.
results.quote:
MOXIE suffered no failures over the course of its 16 
runs on Mars.

results.finding: Hydrogen reduction produced water in seven experiments using a 10 g lunar basalt sample.
results.detail: Water production was monitored and analyzed kinetically, but the text does not demonstrate its electrolysis into oxygen or establish agreement with analytical predictions.
results.quote:
Water production was followed continuously during reduction, and these data were analyzed 
kinetically.

results.finding: One Starship test transferred multiple metric tons of liquid oxygen between tanks in low gravity.
results.detail: The test demonstrated transfer between tanks, but did not demonstrate local production, storage and loading of a lunar ascent vehicle’s mission-scale inventory.
results.quote: The test involved transferring multiple metric tons of cryogenic liquid oxygen between tanks under low-gravity conditions, addressing challenges such as managing the liquid location in the supply tank and preventing vapor pull-through during the transfer process.

results.finding: One Starship test transferred multiple metric tons of liquid oxygen between tanks in low gravity.
results.detail: The test demonstrated transfer between tanks, but did not demonstrate local production, storage and loading of a Mars ascent vehicle’s mission-scale inventory.
results.quote: The test involved transferring multiple metric tons of cryogenic liquid oxygen between tanks under low-gravity conditions, addressing challenges such as managing the liquid location in the supply tank and preventing vapor pull-through during the transfer process.

results.finding: One water-electrolysis system matched predicted performance at 15, 20, and 25 amps.
results.detail: The system was tested in a Mars-environment chamber. The comparison supports the critical oxygen-production function at laboratory proof-of-concept level.
results.quote:
However, results showed that the amount of water electrolyzed 
at 15, 20, and 25 amps was as p redicted, and the data followed a linear trend that projected well to the stated 
performance at the nominal operating condition of 60 amps (Fig. 22).

results.finding: Three Mars propellant-plant systems were tested in a simulated Mars environment.
results.detail: The two carbon-dioxide acquisition alternatives and the electrolysis system were tested separately, not as an integrated resource-to-propellant prototype. Automated separator-level control was also unsuccessful.
results.quote:
This paper presents the test results for three critical systems of a Mars atmospheric processing plant tested in a 
Mars environment simulation chamber.

results.finding: Electrolysis of 30 g JSC-2A lunar regolith simulant removed 96% of its oxygen.
results.detail: Experiments ran at 950 °C. About one-third of the oxygen was detected in the off-gas; the remainder was lost to reactor corrosion. The 96% estimate is based on collected solid product.
results.quote: 96% of the total oxygen was successfully extracted to give a mixed metal alloy product.

results.finding: Molten regolith electrolysis with 25 kg of regolith produced 2.3% oxygen by weight.
results.detail: The experiment ran electrolysis for nine hours in a vacuum chamber. The source does not report that the oxygen-production result supported an analytical prediction, or demonstrate the specified 2020 experiment.
results.quote:
• Key Performance Parameters
• Produced Oxygen 2.3 Weight %

results.finding: Mars atmospheric processing module: four integrated runs each produced methane at 32 g/h.
results.detail: The runs lasted seven hours each. The reported methane production rate matched the stated goal, and the presentation says pure methane was obtained at the expected rate.

results.finding: COPR reactor: 4 carbothermal tests in lunar-relevant thermal vacuum conditions.
results.detail: The tests matured key hardware to TRL 6, but the tested process extracted oxygen as carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. The complete resource-to-propellant system, including conversion to oxygen, was not demonstrated.
results.quote: A total of 4 carbothermal tests were completed in TVAC.

results.finding: One MOXIE instrument produced approximately 50 g of oxygen in seven runs on Mars.
results.detail: MOXIE used carbon dioxide from the martian atmosphere. The paper reports results through 2021, before the later 16-run total.
results.quote: In seven oxygen production runs through 2021, MOXIE successfully produced ~50 g of oxygen and definitively demonstrated that it meets requirements for oxygen generation rate and purity despite design compromises demanded by severe constraints on mass, power, volume, and cost.

results.finding: One MOXIE instrument extracted oxygen from the Martian atmosphere 16 times.
results.detail: MOXIE operated aboard the Perseverance rover on Mars. NASA reported 122 grams of oxygen produced in total.
results.quote: During the mission, MOXIE extracted oxygen from the Martian atmosphere 16 times, testing a way that future astronauts could make rocket propellant that would launch them back to Earth.
